name: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
title: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
answer: In the early grades, most general AI tools are not designed for young children, and the platforms themselves restrict student access, often requiring adult educator accounts or parental consent for students under 13. UNESCO recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI, so a preschooler or first grader is years away from that line. The practical consequence is that AI in preschool through second grade should be teacher-facing, where the benefits are largest and the risks smallest, with the school able to name the adult who set up the tool and the adult who is watching.

sections.body: This idea addresses who is actually allowed to use AI when the learners are very young. Most general AI tools are not built for young children, and the major classroom platforms reflect that: ChatGPT for Teachers is for educators only and offers no student accounts, MagicSchool requires educator accounts to belong to adults with students using it only through a school's own setup, and Canva for Education lets teachers invite students but requires parental consent for those under 13. These platform rules line up with broader guidance, since UNESCO recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI. The problem this solves is the temptation to treat early-grade AI as a student activity when the tools and the guidance both point the other way. The chapter's answer is to keep the work teacher-facing, where the time savings are real and the exposure to young children is minimal.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a preschool through second grade setting, the work sits with the teacher rather than the child. An early childhood teacher spends hours each week on tasks AI does well, such as writing short stories at a child's level, making picture schedules, drafting family notes, and turning scattered observations into clear summaries. Saving even part of that time gives the teacher more minutes on the floor with children, and that trade is the heart of the chapter. The text does not break this down by narrower grade bands within preschool through second grade, so the same teacher-facing pattern applies across the band. Where a school does set up student access through its own system, the text's example is Canva for Education, which requires parental consent for students under 13, and the school should be able to name the adult who set it up and the adult who is watching.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers guidance rather than a study of outcomes. Its stated evidence is UNESCO's recommendation, cited as Miao and Holmes, 2023, that 13 is the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI. The platform details are presented as the rules of the tools themselves: ChatGPT for Teachers is designed for educators only with no student accounts, MagicSchool requires educator accounts to belong to adults with students using it only through a school's own setup, and Canva for Education lets teachers invite students but requires parental consent for students under 13. The claim that teacher use carries the largest benefits and smallest risks is framed as the chapter's reasoning about where time is saved, not as a research finding. No study, figure or measured result beyond the UNESCO age recommendation is given in this text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are age and supervision. UNESCO's recommended minimum of 13 for independent conversations with generative AI means a preschooler or first grader is years away from that line, so independent student use is not the model for this band. Where a school does allow student access through its own setup, as with Canva for Education, parental consent is required for students under 13. The text also sets a supervision standard: when a young child uses an AI tool, the school should be able to name the adult who set it up and the adult who is watching. Those decisions about setup, consent and watching stay with people, not with the tool.
